paragraphs: This position paper argues that scientific datasets cannot always be treated as direct records of the systems being studied. In fields with indirect observation, measurements pass through reconstruction and preprocessing before reaching a learning model. Those steps embody assumptions about how observations relate to reality. Treating the resulting dataset as fixed can hide both those assumptions and uncertainty about alternative processing choices.

The authors identify three problems. A dataset may leave its processing configuration and validity conditions unspecified. A documented pipeline may still lack evidence that it works under changed conditions. Finally, several defensible pipelines may produce different results without that variation entering the scientific uncertainty assessment. A large neuroscience audit stress-tests these concerns, reporting approximately 0.0004% survival under a cross-dataset stability criterion.

The proposed response is to represent pipelines as computable components of inference through domain-specific observation frameworks. This would make their adequacy and stability assessable, turning consequential implementation choices into objects that researchers can audit, reproduce, and incorporate into cumulative evidence.
icml-2026-position-ai-for-science-should.tldr: The authors argue that scientific measurement pipelines must become explicit, testable parts of inference because their choices shape both datasets and uncertainty.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that governing AI across borders requires a shared technical language alongside legal rules. Different jurisdictions have developed their own laws and risk frameworks, creating a fragmented landscape. The authors propose interoperability protocols inspired by international standards, so information about an AI system’s risks can be communicated in consistent, machine-readable forms.

Their central proposal is an AI nutrition label: a standardized manifest reporting comparable information about bias, energy consumption, and the origins of data. Drawing on the relationship between privacy regulation and operational standards, they argue that these labels could make compliance easier across jurisdictions. The intended benefits include less duplicated regulatory work, lower barriers for smaller businesses, and greater public trust.

The paper also addresses the concern that standardization could constrain innovation. It advocates modular protocols with explicit versions that can change as technology develops. The contribution is a governance proposal: technical conformance would provide common ways to describe and assess systems while legal frameworks continue to supply obligations.
icml-2026-position-ai-governance-needs-i.tldr: AI governance should pair laws with evolving, machine-readable standards that make risk information comparable across borders.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the use of AI welfare measurements in governance. Its central argument is that proposed welfare metrics lack an independent validation route: there is no external intervention-based test capable of falsifying them or deciding between competing definitions. On this account, choosing a welfare measure amounts to choosing a mechanism and evaluation convention.

The authors formalize this concern through evaluation theory. Because developers jointly construct the AI system, its behavioral indicators, and the metrics used to judge it, ordinary development choices can create or remove apparent welfare evidence. They then identify two institutional risks: welfare scorecards could add procedural barriers to routine research, and organizations could present discretionary decisions about liability, publicity, or risk as moral requirements.

Their recommendations follow from that diagnosis. They oppose using welfare scores as release gates or invoking model welfare to resist auditing. They argue that restrictions on development should instead rest on externally verifiable harms. These are the paper’s methodological and governance positions, grounded in its critique of welfare validation.
icml-2026-position-ai-welfare-is-bullshi.tldr: The authors argue that untestable AI welfare metrics should not determine release restrictions or obstruct independent oversight.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that strong performance on medical AI benchmarks cannot establish whether a model is ready for clinical deployment. Benchmarks remain useful during development because they help researchers compare methods and identify promising candidates. The authors challenge the further inference that success on a defined test demonstrates usefulness in clinical practice.

The argument draws on a mismatch in both directions. Some models with leading benchmark results have struggled with apparently related clinical tasks, while models with more modest scores have delivered meaningful clinical benefits. That pattern matters because benchmark rankings and practical value can come apart. Selecting a promising model and establishing that it benefits clinical work therefore require different evidence.

The authors call for greater use of measurements grounded in deployment, including prospective studies that assess performance as clinical use unfolds. They also advocate policy changes that reward this kind of evaluation. Their proposed role for benchmarks is a development filter, with deployment decisions supported by evidence that directly addresses clinical readiness.
icml-2026-position-benchmarks-cannot-est.tldr: Medical benchmarks can identify promising AI models, but the authors argue that deployment requires clinically grounded evidence such as prospective studies.

paragraphs: This position paper examines how to create useful synthetic training data when obtaining high-quality labeled examples is difficult or expensive. The authors argue that existing generation, labeling, and adaptation approaches often fail to use the eventual model’s performance as explicit feedback. Consequently, the process of producing data can remain disconnected from what the learner needs.

They propose multi-level optimization as a common framework for coordinating these stages. Data generation would respond to weaknesses such as poor performance on particular classes and inadequate worst-case robustness. Automated labeling would incorporate sequential verification and language models. Adaptation and selection would operate at the level of individual examples, seeking useful training signals while avoiding excessive adaptation.

The key idea is that decisions across the data pipeline should be optimized together using downstream performance. An example’s value would therefore depend on how it helps the model, rather than solely on its properties at creation. The paper presents this coordination as a potential change in how data-scarce domains develop synthetic training sets.
icml-2026-position-creating-high-fidelit.tldr: The authors advocate jointly optimizing synthetic data generation, labeling, adaptation, and selection using feedback from downstream model performance.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for multimodal language models as a more flexible way to predict the functions of DNA, RNA, and proteins. Existing deep learning approaches commonly return predefined categories and require separate training for different tasks. Even multitask systems can remain tied to a fixed task list, while their static predictions offer little opportunity for follow-up exploration.

The proposed alternative uses free-form language to describe complex functional roles and prompts to adapt to new tasks without task-specific retraining. The authors argue that these models can also generalize to biomolecules whose functions are unknown or poorly characterized. This reframes prediction as a context-sensitive explanation that can address questions beyond an established set of labels.

Interactive dialogue is another central feature. Researchers could refine questions, clarify biological context, and explore hypotheses across multiple turns. The paper presents these capabilities as a scalable framework for biomolecular discovery, with relevance to applications such as drug discovery and precision medicine. Its contribution is the case for this adaptable, interactive approach.
icml-2026-position-deciphering-the-funct.tldr: The authors advocate multimodal language models for interactive, free-form biomolecular function prediction and adaptation to new tasks through prompts.

paragraphs: This position paper focuses on the computer environment used by language-model agents performing multistep digital work. The authors argue that existing environments are fragmented and tailored to particular tasks. They propose computers designed around agents, with observations and actions that can be combined and that fit the capabilities of language models.

To make the proposal concrete, they showcase AgentVM, an environment built on a modern operating system. It combines graphical and text-based interaction over a shared system state. Both forms of interaction therefore concern the same underlying computer, while modular environment views organize what the agent can observe and do. This makes the interface itself a central part of agent design.

The paper uses quantitative and qualitative analysis to support its position that a unified environment is essential for general-purpose digital agents. The broader implication is that agent capability depends on how system functionality is exposed, alongside the language model’s abilities. AgentVM illustrates how a common environment can bring different interaction modes into one coherent setting.
icml-2026-position-digital-agents-requir.tldr: The authors present AgentVM to argue that general-purpose digital agents need unified computer environments combining graphical and text interaction.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that AI researchers may encounter obligations under the EU AI Act more often than they expect. Its concern centers on the interaction between research exemptions and publication conventions, especially releasing models and systems. The authors contend that publishing research may remove an exemption and expose researchers to documentation and compliance requirements.

The paper provides a high-level roadmap for assessing whether compliance is needed. It uses ordinary research examples to explain possible applicability and analyzes the structure of research exceptions. A visual navigation tool supports that analysis. Together, these contributions aim to help researchers reason about how their activities and release practices relate to the Act.

The authors also propose legislative changes intended to increase legal certainty and offer two recommendations for reducing noncompliance risk. Their broader position is that the exemption structure may unintentionally disrupt established scientific practices. They frame the paper as a starting point for discussion among researchers, legal scholars, and policymakers about preventing these unintended effects.
icml-2026-position-eu-ai-acts-research-e.tldr: The authors argue that publishing AI models or systems may invalidate research exemptions under the EU AI Act and call for clearer rules.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that providers of training content should receive compensation tied to their measurable contribution to generated outputs. Generative models depend heavily on publicly available material, including copyrighted works, while their outputs can compete with original creations. The authors frame this relationship as an unresolved problem involving economic incentives, ethics, and differing legal treatments.

They examine perspectives on ownership, fair use, and model training, arguing that broad licensing arrangements and one-time payments do not adequately align creators’ and developers’ incentives. Their proposed alternative connects revenue sharing to outcomes at inference time, when a model produces an answer or other output. This makes attribution of contribution central to deciding how compensation should be distributed.

The paper outlines development roadmaps for decentralized systems that perform attribution, accounting, and payouts at scale. The authors argue that fairer distribution could help address disputes and encourage collaboration. By rewarding valuable contributions, the proposed arrangements could also encourage people to produce and share high-quality data, supporting more trustworthy and sustainable generative AI.
icml-2026-position-genai-systems-should-.tldr: The authors propose compensating data providers according to measurable contributions to generated outputs through scalable attribution and revenue-sharing systems.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what changes when people seek information through AI-generated answers instead of ranked search results. Generative Engine Optimization targets both the evidence available to an answer engine and its generation process. The authors analyze this transition to identify how efforts to gain visibility can influence the answers people receive.

They identify concentrated influence when systems are sensitive to optimization and that influence is difficult to contest. They also highlight commercial influence that can enter evidence and reasoning without being disclosed. By formalizing a general optimization pipeline and comparing academic with industry practices, they identify another problem: offline research and deployed systems expose different information and use different evaluation conditions.

The resulting governance proposal focuses on answers themselves. The authors call for stronger opportunities to contest influence, precise disclosure, and black-box audits of material effects on outputs. They also advocate metrics that capture how exposure persists in deployed systems. The central implication is that measuring visibility alone misses how optimization shapes synthesized information.
icml-2026-position-generative-engine-opt.tldr: Optimizing AI answer engines creates risks of concentrated and undisclosed influence that the authors argue require answer-level auditing and governance.

paragraphs: This position paper distinguishes knowing more facts from recognizing the limits of one’s knowledge. The authors argue that much progress in factual question answering has expanded what models know without comparably improving their ability to distinguish knowledge from error. Even frontier models answering straightforward factual questions without external tools still produce incorrect answers.

They conjecture that perfectly separating correct and incorrect responses may be inherently difficult. If so, eliminating errors by withholding answers can reduce usefulness. The paper proposes another framing: treat hallucinations as errors expressed with unjustified confidence. This opens a response option beyond answering confidently or abstaining altogether—communicating uncertainty in a way that faithfully reflects the model’s own uncertainty.

The authors place this capability within metacognition, meaning awareness of uncertainty and action based on it. In direct conversation, that action is honest qualification. In agents, it can guide when to search and which information to trust. Their proposal seeks trustworthy usefulness through better uncertainty awareness, while identifying open problems in achieving that goal.
icml-2026-position-hallucinations-underm.tldr: The authors propose matching expressed uncertainty to a model’s own uncertainty as a way to reduce confident errors while preserving usefulness.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language-model simulations of human behavior need claims and validation matched to the diversity their research questions require. A model can reproduce an average response while failing to reproduce differences among people. The authors describe an average-persona tendency that limits simulations of social dynamics where those differences matter.

They systematically review representative studies and examine the relationship between matching behavioral means and matching behavioral variation. Although most reviewed papers compare their simulations with ground truth, fewer than half explicitly evaluate variance. Among those that do, most report less variation than human populations. The finding suggests that agreement on averages can coexist with a consequential failure to capture population diversity.

The authors recommend reporting variance alongside mean alignment and making validation more demanding when a question depends on heterogeneity. When simulated variation is insufficient, they advise restricting claims to qualitative patterns at the collective level. Their aim is to define productive boundaries for these methods so that the scope of conclusions follows the evidence.
icml-2026-position-llm-based-social-simu.tldr: LLM social simulations should validate behavioral diversity and restrict their claims when they reproduce averages without sufficient human variation.

paragraphs: This position paper distinguishes three activities involved in scientific discovery: learning patterns from observations, deriving consequences from premises, and inventing explanatory premises. The authors argue that generative AI has advanced in the first two but lacks a mechanism for the third, called abduction. They frame this distinction through Einstein’s account of an intuitive jump from experience to axioms.

Using the formulation of general relativity as a computational case study, they challenge the view that creativity can be explained by compressing observed data. Their argument concerns discoveries made with scarce observational evidence. They contend that a modern language model could plausibly carry out deductions from established premises while being structurally unable to generate the abductive jump that establishes those premises.

The paper identifies converting simulation into formal axioms as the critical obstacle for artificial scientific invention. It proposes physically consistent multimodal world models as a source of sensory grounding that could help bridge this divide. The contribution is a conceptual argument about what discovery requires and a proposed direction for supplying that grounding.
icml-2026-position-llms-cant-jump-cddddb.tldr: The authors argue that LLMs lack the abductive mechanism needed to invent scientific premises and propose grounded world models as a path forward.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language models need explicit mechanisms for preserving human perspectives. It defines empathy behaviorally: a model should understand and respond to a person while retaining their intention, emotion, and context. Under this definition, fluent, correct, or policy-compliant language can still distort what a person means.

The authors identify four recurring failures: weakening emotional content, responding at an inappropriate level of emotional detail, avoiding conflict, and creating linguistic distance. They connect these failures to prevailing training and alignment practices and organize them across cognitive, cultural, and relational dimensions. This framework makes empathy a collection of observable response properties that can be examined across tasks.

Their empirical analyses indicate that strong benchmark results can conceal systematic distortions of human perspectives. That finding matters for settings where the meaning of a response depends on whose viewpoint is represented and how it is expressed. The paper calls for empathy-aware objectives, benchmarks, and training signals to become explicit components of model development.
icml-2026-position-llms-should-incorpora.tldr: The authors argue that LLM training and evaluation should explicitly measure and preserve human intention, emotion, and context.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that many failures in systems of collaborating language-model agents are problems of simultaneous access to shared state. Adding agents can reduce reliability when they read and modify the same information concurrently. Long periods spent generating responses increase the chance that an agent acts on information that has changed since it was read.

The authors connect these failures to classical concurrency anomalies: stale reads, overwritten updates, and inconsistent results. This reframing gives a more specific explanation for some problems commonly described as poor coordination or communication. The issue can lie in how actions overlap and interact, even when each agent’s individual reasoning appears adequate.

They advocate explicit mechanisms for detecting conflicts, providing isolation guarantees, and organizing access to shared resources. These mechanisms would make the rules of simultaneous work part of the framework’s design. The broader implication is that improving prompts or model capabilities does not by itself address the shared-state problems identified here; reliable collaboration also requires deliberate control over concurrent operations.
icml-2026-position-multi-agent-systems-s.tldr: Many multi-agent failures arise from concurrent access to shared state, motivating explicit conflict detection, isolation, and resource-access controls.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that detecting AI assistance in peer review does not fully describe its risks. The objective or stance embedded in a prompt can shape a review’s framing and tone. The authors therefore propose auditing prompting intent, focusing on how assistance was directed rather than treating all language-model use as equivalent.

Because real prompting intent is unobserved, they train a detector using generated reviews with synthetic intent labels. They then apply it to ICLR 2026 reviews previously flagged for substantial language-model use. The analysis finds coherent linguistic and structural patterns associated with directional prompting, together with systematic associations involving review ratings, reviewer confidence, and paper acceptance.

These results concern inferred intent and observed associations, so their meaning depends on that distinction from directly inspecting prompts. The practical proposal is to use review text as evidence for an intent-focused auditing process. The authors emphasize transparent procedures and human oversight, positioning the detector as part of a broader examination of how AI assistance influences scientific assessment.
icml-2026-position-prompting-intent-shou.tldr: The authors infer prompting intent from AI-assisted reviews and argue that audits should examine directional influence alongside whether AI was used.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the idea that endangered-language revitalization primarily needs larger datasets, larger models, and broader language coverage. The authors argue that the main constraint lies in how researchers formulate methods and evaluate success. A system can improve an abstract score without adequately serving the language and community it is meant to support.

They draw evidence from language identification, optical character recognition, and synthetic data generation. Across these areas, they describe benchmark-driven scaling as producing brittle or culturally misaligned outcomes when modeling and evaluation do not fit the knowledge and context of the community. The problem concerns the relationship between what a system measures and what meaningful language support requires.

The proposed reorientation places cultural fidelity, community trust, and situated use at the center of evaluation. Progress would be assessed in relation to the particular language and its users. The paper’s broader message is that technical success in revitalization needs community-specific care and appropriate methods, rather than an expectation that greater scale will resolve these mismatches.
icml-2026-position-scale-is-a-false-prom.tldr: The authors argue that endangered-language technology needs culturally grounded methods and evaluation because scale does not resolve misalignment with community needs.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that responsible AI development requires putting data frugality into practice. The authors describe a gap between growing awareness of methods that use less data and continued reliance on ever-larger datasets. Their concern is that diminishing performance gains increasingly come with energy consumption and carbon emissions that development practices do not fully account for.

To ground the argument, they provide indicative estimates of the environmental costs associated with downstream use of ImageNet-1K. They also present empirical evidence for subset selection: choosing a smaller collection of training examples can substantially reduce training energy use while losing little accuracy. Their reported results also show mitigation of dataset bias.

These findings support the practical possibility of reducing data use without a comparable reduction in predictive performance in the examined settings. They also connect data selection to both environmental and bias concerns. The paper closes with actionable recommendations intended to make frugality a concrete development practice, moving beyond general endorsement toward changes in how training data is used.
icml-2026-position-stop-preaching-and-st.tldr: The paper presents evidence that selecting training subsets can substantially reduce energy use with little accuracy loss while mitigating dataset bias.

paragraphs: This position paper treats the growing volume of machine-learning submissions as a research infrastructure problem. Submission growth is outstripping the supply of qualified reviewers, placing pressure on review quality, consistency, and reviewer workload. The authors argue that developing AI assistance for the entire review process should become an urgent community priority.

Their proposed ecosystem assigns language models supporting roles for several participants. Assistants could help verify factual claims, guide reviewer performance, improve manuscripts, and support area chairs making decisions. Human judgment remains central. The proposal therefore concerns a network of complementary forms of assistance across the publication process, rather than a single system responsible for evaluating papers.

The authors identify access to detailed, structured, ethically obtained review-process data as a condition for developing these systems. They outline a research agenda with illustrative experiments for building and validating assistants, while discussing technical and ethical challenges. The intended outcome is a review process that can handle greater scale while preserving the integrity and standards of scientific assessment.
icml-2026-position-the-ml-community-must.tldr: The authors call for an AI-assisted peer-review ecosystem that supports human judgment and is developed using detailed, ethically sourced process data.

paragraphs: This position paper examines a tension in federated learning: hiding individual contributions can also prevent scrutiny of harmful inputs. Secure aggregation makes individual updates cryptographically invisible to the server. The authors argue that unconditional hiding creates a gap in detecting input-level poisoning and undermines the robustness and traceability needed for regulatory compliance.

They propose Controllable Secure Aggregation, which treats access as something governed by fine-grained cryptographic policies. Its proposed stack combines functional encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and threshold cryptography. The intended result preserves server blindness during ordinary operation while allowing a restricted auditing channel for particular inputs when the required consensus is reached.

The authors call this arrangement verified blindness. Its central distinction is that privacy and auditing are built into the same access design: exceptional inspection must follow cryptographically enforced rules rather than unrestricted server discretion. The paper argues that this shift is necessary for robust and trustworthy federated-learning infrastructure. Its contribution is a governance-oriented technical direction for reconciling protected participation with accountable inspection.
icml-2026-position-the-privacy-auditabil.tldr: The authors propose secure aggregation that hides updates by default but permits narrowly governed, consensus-bound audits of specific inputs.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for a precise meaning of machine unlearning in language models. The authors would reserve the term for removing the training influence of a clearly specified dataset, with the resulting model approximately indistinguishable from one retrained without that data. This gives deletion a defined target and a reference model against which to evaluate it.

They distinguish that objective from refusing harmful requests, suppressing particular knowledge, removing entities, or changing targeted behavior. Such tasks may be valuable, but their goals can depend on policy and call for different terminology and comparisons. A model’s decision not to reveal information does not itself establish that the information’s training influence has been removed.

The authors argue that loose terminology leads researchers to reuse metrics beyond their intended scope. Measures of output overlap or forget accuracy can reward surface-level nondisclosure while leaving derived capabilities intact and retraining equivalence untested. They call for evaluations whose guarantees, reference models, and terminology match the actual objective being pursued.
icml-2026-position-the-term-machine-unle.tldr: The authors argue that machine unlearning should mean dataset-defined deletion evaluated against retraining, with behavioral suppression described and tested separately.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that evaluating synthetic speech requires a broader framework as generated voices become increasingly humanlike. Natural-sounding output alone does not capture a system’s capabilities, weaknesses, or societal consequences. The authors introduce responsible evaluation as a way to organize these requirements and guide the next phase of text-to-speech development.

Their framework has three progressive levels. First, objective measurements and human judgments should accurately distinguish capabilities and limitations. Second, standardized benchmarks, transparent reporting, and transferable metrics should enable meaningful comparisons. Third, evaluation should address governance, fairness, and security, including the origins of training data, disparities, misuse, impersonation through spoofing, and traceability.

The authors use this framework to critique current practices, identify systemic shortcomings, and offer recommendations. Its value lies in connecting the quality of a measurement to the decisions it supports: a score should represent the model faithfully, remain useful across comparisons, and address consequences beyond speech quality. The proposed direction aims to support reliable technology and socially beneficial applications.
icml-2026-position-towards-responsible-e.tldr: The authors propose evaluating text-to-speech through faithful capability measurement, comparable reporting, and explicit assessment of societal and security concerns.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that model providers should expose vector prompts as a public interface for customizing language models. Text prompts already influence behavior, but the authors contend that they are inadequate as the sole interface for scalable, stable customization performed without retraining the underlying model. Vector inputs would provide another way to control model behavior.

The authors support their position with diagnostic evidence. In their analysis, vector prompt tuning continues to benefit from more supervision, while text-based prompt optimization reaches a plateau earlier. They also observe dense, global attention patterns for vector prompts, which they interpret as indicating a distinct control mechanism. These findings motivate treating the interface itself as a research and deployment concern.

The paper further discusses why inference-only customization matters under practical deployment constraints. It argues that exposing vector prompts need not fundamentally increase model leakage risk under a standard black-box threat model. That security claim is explicitly tied to the threat model. The broader recommendation is to reconsider which forms of input providers make available for customization.
icml-2026-position-vector-prompt-interfa.tldr: The authors advocate public vector-prompt interfaces, citing diagnostic evidence of improved scaling with supervision and a distinct mechanism for controlling LLM behavior.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the cost of obtaining feedback limits agents in complex domains. Reinforcement-learning successes in relatively inexpensive environments have not readily transferred to robotics, machine-learning engineering, or scientific experimentation. In these settings, taking an action to learn whether it was useful can consume substantial physical resources, time, or experimental capacity.

The authors propose placing world models between agents and the real world. They define these models broadly to include environment dynamics, rewards, and task distributions. Such models could supply learning signals while addressing difficulties associated with learning from actions generated by different policies and with obtaining useful feedback across long sequences of actions.

The paper demonstrates how world models can provide rich learning signals across machine-learning engineering, computer use, robotics, and AI for science. It also identifies challenges in building them and proposes work on dataset curation, architectures, scaling, and evaluation. The central research direction is to improve the intermediary that supplies experience and feedback when direct interaction is expensive.
icml-2026-position-world-models-as-an-in.tldr: The authors propose world models as intermediaries that provide learning signals for agents when real-world actions are costly.

paragraphs: This position paper questions whether vision-language models actually rely on intermediate images in approaches described as thinking with images. These methods insert images produced by tools or code into a reasoning sequence. Their performance improvements, often obtained through reinforcement learning, might appear to show that the model uses those images as part of its reasoning.

The authors present empirical evidence and analysis indicating that intermediate images play little role in the success of the recent methods they examine. They attribute the main gains to changes in language generation produced by fine-tuning. This separates improved task performance from evidence about the mechanism responsible for that improvement.

The authors recommend lightweight ablation studies to test whether the images are necessary, making the contribution of visual information more transparent. They also call for new benchmarks and more informative visual tools. Their position challenges the interpretation of current results: including images within a reasoning sequence does not by itself demonstrate that those images explain the system’s success.
icml-2026-position-your-vlm-may-not-be-t.tldr: The authors find that gains in examined image-interleaved reasoning methods mainly come from improved language generation, motivating tests of whether intermediate images matter.
